intro: Millions of people around the world use healing traditions that are hundreds or thousands of years old. A grandmother in Chicago brews an herbal tea. A doctor in Beijing offers acupuncture after surgery. A family in Tokyo picks up a packet of Kampo herbs from the pharmacy. These traditions carry culture, family memory and real knowledge.

This unit looks at Traditional Chinese Medicine, Ayurveda, Unani, Kampo and healing traditions of the Americas. First you will learn each tradition's ideas in its own terms. Then you will ask the questions scientists ask: What was tested? Compared with what? What did the results show? Some practices, such as tai chi for balance and yoga for back pain, have held up in careful tests. One old recipe led to a Nobel Prize.

By the end, you will be able to explain a tradition respectfully, read a study's result carefully, and name the risks of herbs and supplements. You will also know the single most useful habit for safe care: telling your doctor, nurse or pharmacist about everything you take.
bigQuestion: How can we honor traditional medicine and still let evidence decide what helps?

title: Traditional Medicine and the Evidence

chapters.title: Traditional Chinese Medicine Today
chapters.bigQuestion: How can we respect an old healing tradition and still ask what the evidence shows?

story.title: A Recipe from the Fourth Century
story.kicker: A scientist in Beijing reads an old fever remedy and changes one step in her lab.
paragraphs: In 1969, a scientist named Tu Youyou joined a secret research program in China called Project 523. Its job was to find a new medicine for malaria. Malaria is a disease spread by mosquitoes. The parasite that causes it had learned to survive the drug chloroquine, and soldiers and villagers were getting sick.

Tu and her team searched old medical books and asked practitioners of traditional medicine for remedies. They gathered about 2,000 old recipes and tested extracts from many plants. One plant, qinghao, or sweet wormwood, showed promise in early tests on animals. But the results kept changing. Sometimes the extract worked. Often it did not.

Tu went back to a book by Ge Hong, a Chinese writer of the fourth century. His handbook of emergency remedies said to soak a handful of qinghao in water, wring out the juice and drink it. The recipe did not say to boil the plant. Tu wondered if heat was destroying the active substance.

She changed the method. Her team used a solvent that works at a low temperature. In 1971 the new extract cleared the malaria parasite in mice, and soon after in monkeys. The active chemical was named artemisinin. In 2015, Tu Youyou shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this discovery.
story.think: Tu Youyou used an ancient book and a modern laboratory together. What did each one give her that the other could not?

lessons.title: Qi and the Meridians
lessons.mainIdea: Traditional Chinese Medicine explains health as the smooth flow of qi through channels called meridians.
reading: Picture a clinic in Shanghai. A practitioner takes a patient's pulse at both wrists for a long time. She looks at his tongue. She asks how he sleeps, what he eats and whether he feels hot or cold. These steps come from *Traditional Chinese Medicine*, or TCM, a system of healing developed in China over more than 2,000 years.

TCM teaches that the body is filled with *qi* (said "chee"), often translated as vital energy. In this tradition, qi moves along pathways called *meridians*. Health means qi flows smoothly and stays in balance. Illness means qi is blocked, too weak or out of balance. Treatments such as acupuncture, herbs and exercise aim to restore that flow.

Qi and meridians are ideas inside the TCM framework. Scientists have not found meridians as physical structures, and qi has not been measured as a form of energy. That does not mean a treatment is useless. It means we test each treatment by its results in people, not by whether its explanation matches modern biology.

words.d: a system of healing developed in China over many centuries, using herbs, acupuncture, diet and exercise
in TCM, the vital energy believed to flow through the body
in TCM, the channels through which qi is said to flow

look.title: Two Ways to Describe a Headache
look.text: A TCM practitioner might say a patient's headache comes from blocked qi in certain meridians. A family doctor might say the same headache comes from tight neck muscles and too little sleep. Both are trying to explain the same pain. Each uses the ideas of its own system.
look.prompt: How could a researcher test a headache treatment fairly, even if the two explanations disagree?

check.q: In TCM, what does it mean when qi flows smoothly and in balance?
check.why: TCM teaches that health is the smooth, balanced flow of qi through the meridians.

check.why: The reading says meridians are ideas in the TCM framework and have not been found as physical structures.

lessons.title: Yin, Yang and Five Phases
lessons.mainIdea: TCM uses yin-yang and the five phases to describe balance and change in the body.
reading: Think of a day. Morning light grows, noon is bright and hot, and evening cools into a dark night. Chinese thinkers used this kind of pattern to describe *yin and yang*. Yin stands for cool, dark, still and inward qualities. Yang stands for warm, bright, active and outward qualities. Each needs the other, and each slowly turns into the other.

TCM applies this idea to the body. A person with a high fever, a red face and a fast pulse may be described as having too much yang. A person who feels cold, tired and pale may be described as having too much yin. The practitioner then chooses herbs or foods that are said to cool or warm, bringing the two back into balance.

TCM also uses the *five phases*: wood, fire, earth, metal and water. Each phase is linked to organs, seasons, colors and emotions. In the tradition, the phases support and control one another in cycles. These are ways of organizing observations, like a map. Modern medicine uses a different map, based on cells, chemistry and experiments.

words.d: in Chinese thought, two opposite but linked qualities, such as cool and warm, that must stay in balance
in TCM, wood, fire, earth, metal and water, used to link organs, seasons and emotions
a set of ideas used to organize and explain observations

lessons.title: TCM in China's Hospitals
lessons.mainIdea: In China, TCM and Western medicine are often practiced side by side, sometimes in the same hospital.
reading: Walk into a large hospital in Beijing and you may find two pharmacies. One hands out pills made in factories. The other has rows of drawers filled with dried roots, bark and flowers. In China, many hospitals offer both Western medicine and TCM, and many doctors are trained in both.

After 1949, the government of the People's Republic of China supported TCM and built colleges to train its practitioners. It also encouraged *integration*, meaning TCM and Western medicine working together. A patient might have surgery for a broken hip and also receive acupuncture or herbal tea during recovery.

TCM is also used far beyond China. Acupuncture clinics exist in cities across the United States, including Chicago. In the U.S., each state decides who may practice acupuncture and what training is required. Researchers in China and around the world now run clinical trials to test which TCM treatments help, and for what.

words.d: using two systems of medicine together in the care of one patient
a careful study that tests a treatment in people and compares the results
a person trained to practice a system of healing

lessons.title: Acupuncture and Chronic Pain
lessons.mainIdea: Studies suggest acupuncture may help some people with some kinds of chronic pain and nausea.
reading: Maria, a nurse, has had low back pain for more than a year. Her doctor suggests physical therapy, and she also tries *acupuncture*. In acupuncture, a trained practitioner places very thin needles into the skin at chosen points. Many patients say it feels like a small tap or a dull ache, not like a shot.

Researchers have studied acupuncture in thousands of patients with *chronic pain*, which is pain that lasts three months or longer. Large reviews of these trials suggest that acupuncture may help some people with back pain, neck pain, knee arthritis and headaches. The benefit is usually modest, not dramatic. Some people improve a lot, and some not at all.

Acupuncture has also been tested for nausea. Studies of pressing or needling a point on the inner wrist suggest it may reduce nausea after surgery for some patients. Acupuncture is usually safe when done by a licensed practitioner with clean, single-use needles. Anyone thinking about it should talk with a doctor first.

words.d: a treatment in which thin needles are placed into the skin at chosen points
pain that lasts three months or longer
small or moderate, not large

look.title: What a U.S. Health Agency Says

It may also help reduce how often tension headaches happen and prevent some migraines. It is generally safe when done by an experienced practitioner using sterile needles.
look.cite: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH), "Acupuncture: What You Need To Know," fact sheet, about 2022

lessons.title: What Sham Trials Show
lessons.mainIdea: In many trials, fake acupuncture works almost as well as real acupuncture, which raises questions about how it helps.
reading: How do you test a needle treatment fairly? In a *sham* trial, one group gets real acupuncture. Another group gets a fake version. The fake might use needles placed at the wrong points, or blunt needles that touch the skin but do not go in. Patients do not know which group they are in.

Many sham-controlled trials find that real and sham acupuncture give similar results. Both groups often feel better than people who get no acupuncture at all. When real acupuncture does beat sham, the difference is usually small. This tells researchers that much of the benefit may come from the whole experience, not the exact needle points.

Part of that experience is the *placebo effect*: real improvement that comes from expecting to get better and from caring attention. Placebo effects are real for symptoms such as pain. Scientists still debate what these results mean. Some say acupuncture works mainly through placebo. Others say needling any spot may have real effects on nerves.

words.d: a fake treatment made to look like the real one, used for comparison in a study
real improvement in symptoms that comes from expecting to get better and from care, not from the treatment itself
describes a study in which patients do not know which treatment they received

look.title: Three Groups
look.text: A study of 300 people with knee pain splits them into three groups. Group A gets real acupuncture. Group B gets sham acupuncture with needles at the wrong points. Group C stays on a waiting list. After eight weeks, A and B both report less pain than C. A reports only a little less pain than B.
look.prompt: What can the researchers conclude from comparing A with B, and A with C?

check.q: What is a sham treatment in a study?
choices: A fake version made to look like the real treatment
A treatment given only to doctors
A treatment that has been banned
check.why: A sham is a fake treatment made to look real, used for comparison.

check.q: What do many sham-controlled acupuncture trials find?
choices: Sham works far better than real acupuncture

check.why: The reading says many trials find real and sham acupuncture give similar results.

check.q: Why do researchers use blinded studies?
choices: So patients' expectations do not decide which group looks better

check.why: Blinding keeps expectations, part of the placebo effect, from tilting the results toward one group.

lessons.title: Tai Chi for Balance
lessons.mainIdea: Tai chi, a slow Chinese exercise, has good evidence for improving balance and preventing falls in older adults.
reading: Early in the morning in a park in Chicago's Chinatown, a group of older adults move together in slow, flowing steps. They shift weight from one foot to the other and turn their arms in wide circles. This is *tai chi*, a mind-body exercise that began in China as a martial art.

In TCM, tai chi is said to help qi flow. Scientists have studied it in a different way, by counting falls. Falls are a leading cause of injury in older adults. Many trials show that regular tai chi improves *balance* and leg strength. Reviews of these trials find that exercise programs that include tai chi lower the number of falls in older people.

Because of this evidence, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention lists tai chi among programs that can help prevent falls. Tai chi is gentle, and people can adjust it for their own bodies. It shows how a traditional practice can earn a place in modern care by passing careful tests.

words.d: a slow, flowing Chinese exercise that joins movement, breathing and focus
the ability to keep the body steady and upright
steps taken to lower the chance that a person falls and gets hurt

sections.title: From Old Text to New Drug

lessons.title: Tu Youyou and Project 523
lessons.mainIdea: Tu Youyou used an ancient text as a clue and modern chemistry as a test to discover artemisinin.
reading: In the 1960s, malaria was killing soldiers and civilians in Southeast Asia. The malaria parasite had become resistant to chloroquine, the main drug of the time. *Resistance* means the germ is no longer killed by a medicine that used to work. China started a secret program, Project 523, to find new drugs.

Tu Youyou's team gathered more than 2,000 old recipes and tested extracts from about 200 herbs. Sweet wormwood looked promising but gave uneven results. Tu reread a fourth-century handbook by Ge Hong, which described soaking the herb in water, with no boiling. She guessed that heat was breaking down the active chemical, so she used a low-temperature *extraction* with a solvent called ether.

The new extract worked in animals in 1971. The team then tested it in people, including themselves, to check safety. Chemists found the structure of the active molecule, *artemisinin*. The old book gave the clue. Careful lab work, animal tests and clinical trials turned the clue into a proven medicine.

words.d: when a germ is no longer killed by a medicine that used to work against it
a method for pulling a chemical out of a plant or other material
a malaria drug first isolated from sweet wormwood by Tu Youyou's team

look.title: Ge Hong's Instruction
look.text: Take a handful of qinghao, soak it in about two liters of water, wring out the juice and drink all of it.
look.cite: Ge Hong, Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies, c. 340 CE, as described by Tu Youyou in her 2015 Nobel lecture
look.prompt: Which detail in this instruction gave Tu Youyou the idea to avoid heat?

choices: To find new malaria drugs because the parasite resisted chloroquine
check.why: Project 523 searched for new malaria drugs after the parasite became resistant to chloroquine.

check.q: What change did Tu Youyou make after rereading Ge Hong?
choices: She switched to a different plant
check.why: Ge Hong described soaking, not boiling, so Tu used a low-temperature method with ether.

check.q: What turned the old clue into a proven medicine?
choices: Lab work, animal tests and clinical trials

check.why: The reading says careful lab work, animal tests and clinical trials made the clue a proven medicine.

lessons.title: Artemisinin in the World
lessons.mainIdea: Artemisinin-based combination therapies are now a main treatment for malaria and have saved many lives.
reading: Today a child with malaria in Nigeria or Uganda is often treated with an *artemisinin-based combination therapy*, or ACT. An ACT pairs a drug made from artemisinin with a second malaria drug. The World Health Organization recommends ACTs as a first-line treatment for the most common dangerous type of malaria.

Why combine two drugs? Artemisinin clears parasites very fast, but it leaves the body quickly. The partner drug lasts longer and kills parasites that remain. Using two drugs together also makes it harder for the parasite to develop resistance, because it would need to resist both at once.

In 2015, Tu Youyou shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with William Campbell and Satoshi Omura, who discovered a drug against parasitic worms. Tu was the first Chinese woman to win a Nobel Prize in science. Her story shows that a *traditional remedy* can hold a real clue, but the clue must be tested.

words.d: a malaria treatment that pairs an artemisinin drug with a longer-lasting partner drug
the treatment doctors are advised to try first for a condition
a treatment passed down within a healing tradition

rows: Share of deaths in WHO African Region (%)

choices: An artemisinin drug paired with a partner malaria drug

check.q: Why does combining two malaria drugs help slow resistance?

check.q: Who shared the 2015 Nobel Prize with Tu Youyou?

lessons.title: Herbs, Drugs and Contamination
lessons.mainIdea: Herbal products can interact with medicines or be contaminated, so tell your doctor about any herbs you take.
reading: Mr. Chen takes a blood thinner after a heart problem. His cousin mails him a box of herbal tea said to help circulation. Some herbs can change how a medicine works in the body. This is called a *herb-drug interaction*. A few herbs may add to a blood thinner's effect and raise the risk of bleeding.

Another risk is *contamination*. In some tests of herbal products, including some sold as TCM, researchers have found lead, mercury or arsenic. Others have found hidden prescription drugs or the wrong plant. In the 1990s, patients in Belgium had serious kidney damage after taking a slimming product that contained a plant with aristolochic acid.

"Natural" does not always mean safe. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration does not approve herbal *supplements* for safety and effectiveness before they are sold, as it does for medicines. That is why the best step is simple: tell your doctor or pharmacist about every herb, tea and supplement you use.

words.d: a change in how a medicine works because of an herb taken at the same time
the presence of something harmful or unexpected in a product
products such as herbs, vitamins or extracts taken by mouth to add to the diet

lessons.title: Endangered Animals and Respect
lessons.mainIdea: Some traditional products use endangered animals, and respectful talk about TCM includes this problem and the evidence.
reading: A ranger in Africa guards a rhinoceros through the night. Poachers kill rhinos for their horns, which are sold in some markets as traditional medicine. Tiger bone and pangolin scales have also been sold this way. These animals are now *endangered*, which means they are at risk of dying out.

An international treaty called *CITES* controls trade in endangered wildlife, and most countries have signed it. Rhino horn is made of keratin, the same protein as fingernails. There is no good scientific evidence that it treats disease. Many TCM practitioners and organizations support using plant or farmed substitutes instead of wild animals.

Talking about TCM fairly means holding two ideas at once. The tradition has deep roots and has given the world real gifts, such as artemisinin and tai chi. Some of its products also have risks or lack evidence. *Evidence-based* discussion respects the people who use TCM by asking the same careful questions of every treatment, Eastern or Western.

words.d: at risk of dying out as a species
an international treaty that controls trade in endangered plants and animals
based on careful studies of what works, rather than only on tradition or opinion

choices: Tell the doctor or pharmacist about the tea
Double the tea to be sure it works
Say nothing because it is natural
review.why: Herbs can interact with medicines, so the chapter advises telling a doctor or pharmacist.

review.q: How do TCM and Western medicine often relate in China's hospitals?
choices: They are often practiced side by side
review.why: Many Chinese hospitals offer both, and many doctors are trained in both.

chapters.title: Ayurveda, Unani and Other Traditions
chapters.bigQuestion: How can patients and doctors share what they know about traditional remedies so that care stays safe?

story.title: The Herbs in the Suitcase
story.kicker: A heart doctor in Chicago learns that the most important question is the one nobody asked.
paragraphs: On a gray morning in a Chicago clinic, a cardiologist, or heart doctor, meets a new patient. Mrs. Rao is sixty-two. Her blood pressure has been high, and her last doctor started her on a medicine for it. She brings a neat list of her pills. It looks complete.

The doctor asks one more question. "Do you take any herbs, teas or supplements, even ones from home?" Mrs. Rao smiles and nods. Every few months her mother mails a package from India. Inside are powders and tablets from an Ayurvedic shop, meant to keep her strong and calm. She never thought to mention them.

The doctor does not scold her. She asks to see the labels and writes down each name. She explains that some herbs can change how heart medicines work. She also explains that a few imported products have been found to contain lead or mercury. She suggests they check the products together, with a pharmacist.

Mrs. Rao feels respected. Her family's tradition matters to her, and her doctor treats it that way. Together they make a plan that keeps what is safe and helpful, and checks what is not known. The whole change came from one friendly question.
story.think: Why do you think Mrs. Rao never mentioned her herbs? What made her feel comfortable telling the doctor?

lessons.title: The Three Doshas
lessons.mainIdea: Ayurveda teaches that health depends on the balance of three doshas: vata, pitta and kapha.
reading: In a clinic in Kerala, in southern India, a practitioner asks a new patient about her sleep, her digestion and her moods. She notes that the patient is thin, moves quickly and often feels cold. These questions come from *Ayurveda*, a healing tradition from India whose classic texts are about 2,000 years old. Its name means "knowledge of life."

Ayurveda holds that each body is shaped by three *doshas*, or forces. Vata is linked to air and movement. Pitta is linked to fire and digestion. Kapha is linked to earth, water and structure. In the tradition, each person is born with their own mix, called their *prakriti*, or constitution.

Ayurveda teaches that illness comes when the doshas fall out of balance. The practitioner in Kerala might say her patient has a lot of vata and suggest warm food and a regular routine. Like qi in Chinese medicine, the doshas are ideas within the tradition. They have not been measured as physical substances.

words.d: a traditional system of medicine from India; its name means knowledge of life
in Ayurveda, the three forces, vata, pitta and kapha, said to shape the body and mind
in Ayurveda, a person's natural mix of the three doshas from birth

look.title: Three Descriptions
look.text: An Ayurvedic practitioner describes three people. The first is quick, creative and often cold. The second is focused, warm and has a strong appetite. The third is calm, steady and sleeps deeply. In Ayurveda, each description points to one dosha being strongest.
look.prompt: Using the reading, match each person to vata, pitta or kapha. Which clues did you use?

check.q: What does the word Ayurveda mean?
check.why: The reading says Ayurveda means knowledge of life.

check.q: In Ayurveda, which dosha is linked to fire and digestion?
check.why: Ayurveda links pitta to fire and digestion.

check.q: How does the reading describe the doshas?
choices: As ideas within the tradition, not measured substances
As chemicals found in blood tests
check.why: The reading says the doshas are ideas within the tradition and have not been measured as physical substances.

lessons.title: Diet and Daily Routine
lessons.mainIdea: Ayurveda gives great weight to food, sleep and a steady daily routine.
reading: Before sunrise, an Ayurvedic daily plan might begin with waking early, rinsing the mouth, drinking warm water and stretching. This routine is called *dinacharya*, or daily practice. Ayurveda teaches that doing the same healthy things at the same times each day helps keep the doshas in balance.

Food is central. Ayurveda sorts foods by six tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent and astringent. A practitioner may suggest more warm, cooked food for a person with strong vata, or cooling foods for strong pitta. Meals are meant to be eaten calmly, at regular times, with the largest meal near midday.

Some of this advice overlaps with modern *lifestyle medicine*, which studies how sleep, diet, activity and stress affect health. Regular sleep, plenty of vegetables and calm meals are supported by many studies. The dosha reasons behind the advice are the tradition's own. The habits themselves can be tested and often hold up well.

words.d: in Ayurveda, a healthy daily routine done at regular times
a field of modern medicine that studies how daily habits like sleep, diet and activity affect health
a set of actions done regularly in the same order

look.title: Same Habit, Two Reasons
look.text: An Ayurvedic practitioner tells a student to go to bed and wake at the same time each day to calm vata. A school nurse tells the same student to keep a regular sleep schedule because it helps the body clock and makes it easier to focus in class.
look.prompt: The reasons differ, but the advice matches. How could you test whether the habit helps, no matter which reason is right?

check.q: What is dinacharya?
check.why: Dinacharya is the Ayurvedic daily routine done at regular times.

check.q: How many tastes does Ayurveda use to sort foods?
check.why: Ayurveda sorts foods by six tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent and astringent.

check.q: What does modern lifestyle medicine study?
choices: How habits like sleep, diet and activity affect health
check.why: Lifestyle medicine studies how daily habits affect health.

lessons.title: India's Ministry of AYUSH
lessons.mainIdea: India's government recognizes Ayurveda and several other traditions through its Ministry of AYUSH.
reading: In India, a young person can go to college for five years or more to become an Ayurvedic doctor. These colleges are regulated by the national government. In 2014, India created the *Ministry of AYUSH*, a government ministry for traditional systems of medicine.

AYUSH stands for Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy. The ministry funds research, sets standards for training and supports hospitals and clinics. Millions of people in India use these systems, often together with modern medicine. Government recognition means these systems are part of public health care in India.

*Recognition* by a government is different from scientific proof. It shows that a society values a tradition and wants it to be taught and regulated. Whether a specific remedy works for a specific illness still has to be tested in fair trials. India's own researchers run many such trials, and results vary from treatment to treatment.

words.d: the Indian government ministry for Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy
official approval by a government that a practice may be taught and used
to control something with official rules

look.title: Recognized or Proven?
look.text: A news headline reads: "Government recognizes traditional medicine." A student says this means every traditional remedy has been proven to work. Her classmate disagrees and says recognition and proof are two different things.
look.prompt: Which student is right, based on the reading? Give a reason.

check.q: In what year did India create the Ministry of AYUSH?
check.why: The reading says India created the Ministry of AYUSH in 2014.

check.q: Which tradition is included in AYUSH?
check.why: AYUSH stands for Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy.

check.q: How is government recognition different from scientific proof?
choices: They mean exactly the same thing
Recognition means every remedy is proven
Recognition shows a society values a tradition; proof comes from fair trials
Proof comes from a government vote
check.why: The reading says recognition shows value and regulation, while proof requires fair trials.

lessons.title: Yoga and Low Back Pain
lessons.mainIdea: Yoga can help some adults with chronic low back pain a little, about as much as other exercise.
reading: James drives a delivery truck and has had low back pain for months. His doctor suggests a weekly *yoga* class designed for back pain. Yoga began in India as a spiritual practice. It joins body postures, breathing and focused attention. Many people today practice it mainly for health.

Researchers have tested yoga in many trials of adults with chronic low back pain. Reviews of these trials find that yoga can lower pain and improve daily function a small to moderate amount, about as much as other exercise programs. In 2017, the American College of Physicians advised doctors to try non-drug options such as exercise, yoga and tai chi first for chronic low back pain.

Yoga is not a cure-all. Some poses can strain the body, so beginners do best with a trained teacher who can adjust poses. People with health conditions should ask their doctor first. Yoga shows how a practice from one tradition can pass modern tests for a specific *indication*, which means a specific use.

words.d: a practice from India that joins body postures, breathing and focused attention
a specific health problem for which a treatment is used
official advice to doctors about how to treat a condition, based on reviewed evidence

look.title: A Doctors' Group Weighs In
look.text: For patients with chronic low back pain, doctors should first choose treatments without drugs. Options include exercise, rehabilitation, acupuncture, mindfulness-based stress reduction, tai chi, yoga and spinal manipulation, among others.
look.cite: American College of Physicians, clinical practice guideline on low back pain (Qaseem et al.), Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017
look.prompt: Which practices in this guideline come from traditions discussed in this unit?

check.q: How large is yoga's benefit for chronic low back pain, according to reviews?
choices: Small to moderate, about like other exercise
check.why: Reviews find yoga gives a small to moderate benefit, about as much as other exercise programs.

check.q: What did the American College of Physicians advise in 2017?
choices: Try non-drug options like yoga first for chronic low back pain
check.why: The 2017 guideline advised starting with non-drug options such as exercise, yoga and tai chi.

check.q: What is an indication?
choices: A sign on a clinic door
A specific use for which a treatment is given
check.why: An indication is a specific health problem for which a treatment is used.

lessons.title: Meditation and Stress
lessons.mainIdea: Meditation programs have evidence for easing stress and anxiety for some people.
reading: Before a big exam, Aisha sits quietly for ten minutes. She breathes slowly and notices her thoughts without chasing them. This is a form of *meditation*, a practice of training attention. Meditation has roots in several Asian traditions, including those of India, and is part of Ayurvedic and yogic teaching.

Scientists have tested meditation programs, especially *mindfulness*, which means paying calm attention to the present moment. A large review published in 2014 in JAMA Internal Medicine found moderate evidence that mindfulness programs can ease anxiety, depression and pain for some adults. The effects were similar in size to some other helpful treatments.

Meditation is low-risk for most people and costs little. It is a tool, not a replacement for care. Someone who feels very anxious or sad for a long time should talk with a trusted adult, a school counselor or a doctor. Meditation can work alongside that support, and many people find it helps them feel steady.

words.d: a practice of training attention, often by focusing on the breath
paying calm attention to the present moment without judging it
a feeling of worry or unease, often about what might happen

look.title: Complementary Health Practices Used by U.S. Adults, 2012
rows: Yoga, tai chi or qi gong
look.unit: percent of U.S. adults in past year
look.cite: Clarke et al., National Health Statistics Reports no. 79, CDC National Center for Health Statistics, 2015 (2012 survey)
look.prompt: Which two practices from this chapter's traditions appear in the table? About what share of adults used each?

check.q: What is mindfulness?
choices: Holding one's breath as long as possible
Paying calm attention to the present moment
check.why: Mindfulness means paying calm attention to the present moment without judging it.

check.q: What did a large 2014 review find about mindfulness programs?
choices: Moderate evidence that they ease anxiety, depression and pain for some adults
check.why: The 2014 review found moderate evidence of benefit for anxiety, depression and pain.

check.q: What should someone do if they feel very anxious or sad for a long time?
choices: Talk with a trusted adult, counselor or doctor
Only meditate and tell no one
check.why: The reading says meditation is a tool, not a replacement for care, and to talk with a trusted adult or doctor.

lessons.title: Turmeric in the Lab and in People
lessons.mainIdea: Curcumin from turmeric looks promising in lab studies, but proof of benefit in people is limited.
reading: Turmeric is the golden spice that colors many curries. Ayurveda has used it for centuries for digestion, skin and aches. Its best-known chemical is *curcumin*. In lab dishes and animal studies, curcumin has shown effects on inflammation, which is the body's response to injury or infection.

Results in a lab dish do not always carry over to people. Curcumin is poorly absorbed by the gut and breaks down quickly in the body. That means very little may reach the tissues. Many human trials of curcumin have been small or short, and their results are mixed. A few suggest it may ease knee arthritis pain a little, but those studies are not strong. The U.S. National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health says there is little reliable evidence for most uses.

Some chemists have warned that curcumin can look active in many lab tests for reasons that do not mean it works as a drug. This is a lesson about *preclinical* research: early lab and animal studies are a starting point, not an answer. Turmeric in food is generally safe, but supplements can interact with some medicines, so tell your doctor.

words.d: the main studied chemical in turmeric
the body's response to injury or infection, with swelling, heat or redness
describes early research in lab dishes or animals, before testing in people

look.title: From Dish to Person
look.text: A headline says: "Spice chemical fights inflammation!" The study behind it tested curcumin on cells in a plastic dish. No people took part. A reader wonders whether she should buy curcumin pills for her sore knees.
look.prompt: What questions should the reader ask before trusting this headline? Use the word preclinical in your answer.

check.q: Why might curcumin do less in people than in a lab dish?
choices: It is poorly absorbed and breaks down quickly
check.why: The reading says curcumin is poorly absorbed by the gut and breaks down quickly.

check.q: What is preclinical research?
choices: Large trials in thousands of people
Early studies in lab dishes or animals
Research done only by doctors in clinics
check.why: Preclinical research means early lab and animal studies before testing in people.

check.q: What does the NCCIH say about curcumin for most uses?
choices: It is proven to cure arthritis
It is banned in the U.S.
check.why: The reading says the NCCIH finds little reliable evidence for most uses.

lessons.title: Heavy Metals in Some Products
lessons.mainIdea: Some imported Ayurvedic products have been found to contain lead, mercury or arsenic.
reading: In some Ayurvedic practice, metals and minerals are processed into preparations called *rasa shastra* medicines. The tradition teaches that careful processing makes them safe. Testing tells a more worrying story. Some of these products, and some herbal ones too, have been found to contain *heavy metals*, such as lead, mercury and arsenic.

In 2008, researchers led by Robert Saper tested Ayurvedic products bought online. Published in JAMA, the study found that about one in five contained detectable lead, mercury or arsenic. Products made in India and products made in the U.S. both had problems. Doctors have reported cases of lead poisoning in people who took such products.

Lead can harm the brain, kidneys and blood, and children are most sensitive to it. This does not mean every Ayurvedic product is unsafe. It means *quality control* matters. Buy from trusted sources, show products to a pharmacist, and tell your doctor, who can order a simple blood test for lead if needed.

words.d: metals such as lead, mercury and arsenic that can be harmful to the body
a branch of Ayurveda that prepares medicines using metals and minerals
checks that make sure a product contains what it should and nothing harmful

look.title: Metals in Ayurvedic Products Bought Online
rows: Rasa shastra products (made with metals on purpose)
look.unit: percent of products with detectable lead, mercury or arsenic
look.cite: Saper et al., Lead, Mercury, and Arsenic in US- and Indian-Manufactured Ayurvedic Medicines Sold via the Internet, JAMA, 2008
look.prompt: Which kind of product most often contained metals? Using the reading, explain why that might be, and what a buyer should do.

check.q: What did the 2008 Saper study find?
choices: About one in five products contained lead, mercury or arsenic
check.why: The 2008 JAMA study found about one in five products contained a heavy metal.

check.q: What is rasa shastra?
choices: A branch of Ayurveda that uses metals and minerals
check.why: Rasa shastra is the branch of Ayurveda that prepares medicines with metals and minerals.

check.q: Who is most sensitive to harm from lead?
check.why: The reading says children are most sensitive to lead.

lessons.title: Unani Medicine
lessons.mainIdea: Unani medicine grew from Greek ideas carried forward by Arabic and Persian physicians and is practiced today in South Asia.
reading: In Delhi, a patient visits a *hakim*, a practitioner of Unani medicine. The hakim asks about his temperament and diet and may suggest herbs, a change in food or rest. The word Unani comes from the Arabic word for Greek. The system began with Greek medicine, especially the ideas of Hippocrates and Galen.

Physicians in the Islamic world translated, tested and expanded these Greek ideas. The Persian physician Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, wrote the *Canon of Medicine* around 1025. It was used as a medical textbook in Europe and the Middle East for centuries. Unani medicine kept the Greek idea of four humors, the body fluids once thought to control health.

Western medicine gave up the four humors in the 1800s, after experiments showed how germs and cells cause disease. Unani medicine still uses humors as its framework. Today it is practiced mainly in India, Pakistan and nearby countries, and it is part of India's AYUSH ministry. As with any tradition, each remedy should be judged by fair tests.

words.d: a tradition based on Greek medicine as developed by Arabic and Persian physicians
a practitioner of Unani medicine
blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile, once thought to control health
a large medical textbook written by Ibn Sina around 1025

look.title: One Idea, Two Paths
look.text: Around 1400, a doctor in Paris and a doctor in Cairo might both explain a fever using the four humors, and both might study Ibn Sina's Canon. By 1900, the Paris doctor's successors used germ theory. Many hakims in South Asia kept the humors as their framework.
look.prompt: Why might two groups that started from the same idea end up in such different places?

check.q: What does the word Unani refer to?
check.why: Unani comes from the Arabic word for Greek, because the system began with Greek medicine.

check.q: Who wrote the Canon of Medicine around 1025?
check.why: The Persian physician Ibn Sina, or Avicenna, wrote the Canon of Medicine.

check.q: What framework does Unani medicine still use?
check.why: Unani medicine kept the Greek idea of the four humors as its framework.

lessons.title: Kampo in Japan
lessons.mainIdea: Kampo is Japan's adaptation of Chinese herbal medicine, and many Kampo formulas are used within Japan's national health system.
reading: In a Tokyo clinic, a doctor trained in Western medicine writes a prescription for a packet of powdered herbs. This is *Kampo*, Japanese herbal medicine. Kampo came to Japan from China more than 1,000 years ago. Over the centuries, Japanese doctors adapted it, simplified many formulas and developed their own ways of diagnosing.

Kampo is unusual because it is part of mainstream care. Since the 1970s, Japan's national health insurance has covered many Kampo formulas, which are made in factories to set standards. In Japan, Kampo is usually prescribed by medical doctors, not by a separate group of practitioners. Many doctors use Kampo alongside modern drugs.

Researchers in Japan study Kampo formulas in clinical trials. Some show benefits for specific uses, while others have little evidence. Like any medicine, Kampo can cause *side effects*. For example, some formulas contain licorice, which in large amounts can raise blood pressure and lower potassium. That is why doctors track Kampo like any other prescription.

words.d: Japanese herbal medicine adapted from Chinese medicine
unwanted effects of a medicine besides the one intended
a government program that helps pay for people's medical care

look.title: Comparing Two Systems
look.text: In China, many hospitals have a separate TCM department with its own doctors. In Japan, the same family doctor may prescribe an antibiotic for one patient and a Kampo formula for the next. Both countries use herbal medicine from the same Chinese roots.
look.prompt: What is one advantage of having the same doctor prescribe both kinds of medicine?

check.q: Where did Kampo come from?
check.why: Kampo came to Japan from China and was adapted by Japanese doctors.

check.q: Who usually prescribes Kampo in Japan?
check.why: In Japan, Kampo is usually prescribed by medical doctors.

check.q: Why must doctors watch for licorice in some Kampo formulas?
choices: It is an endangered animal product
In large amounts it can raise blood pressure and lower potassium
check.why: The reading says licorice in large amounts can raise blood pressure and lower potassium.

sections.title: Healing in the Americas and Today

lessons.title: Indigenous and Curandero Traditions
lessons.mainIdea: Indigenous healers and curanderos in the Americas treat body, mind, family and spirit together.
reading: In the Pilsen neighborhood of Chicago, a small shop called a *botanica* sells dried herbs, candles and teas. Some families visit a *curandero* or curandera, a traditional healer in Mexican and other Latin American communities. Curanderismo mixes herbal knowledge, prayer and practices from Indigenous, Spanish and African roots.

Across North and South America, Indigenous nations have their own healing traditions. These differ from nation to nation, and many are private to each community. They often treat a person's health as linked to family, community, land and spirit. Some U.S. health programs that serve Native American communities now include traditional healers in patient care when patients ask for them.

Respect matters here. Many of these traditions were once banned or mocked. Doctors now learn *cultural humility*, which means listening and learning from each patient instead of assuming. Some herbs used in these traditions have been studied and some have not. A good doctor asks about them openly, so patients feel safe telling the whole story.

words.d: a traditional healer in Mexican and other Latin American communities
a shop that sells herbs, candles and items used in traditional healing
a practice of listening to and learning from each patient's culture instead of assuming

look.title: A Grandmother's Tea
look.text: A teen in Chicago has a stomachache. His grandmother makes him a tea from an herb bought at a botanica, the way her mother did in Mexico. The next week, his doctor asks what helped. The teen is not sure whether he should mention the tea.
look.prompt: How could the doctor ask so that the teen feels comfortable sharing? Why would it help?

choices: A shop that sells herbs and items for traditional healing

check.q: Which roots does curanderismo draw from, according to the reading?

check.q: What is cultural humility?

Assuming you already know a patient's beliefs
Listening to and learning from each patient's culture

lessons.title: Integrative Clinics and Telling Your Doctor
lessons.mainIdea: Integrative medicine combines proven complementary practices with standard care, and it starts with telling your doctor everything you take.
reading: At a large cancer center, a patient finishing chemotherapy meets with a team. One person teaches gentle yoga. Another offers acupuncture for nausea. A dietitian plans meals. Her cancer doctor leads the plan. This is *integrative medicine*, which combines standard care with complementary practices that have evidence for a specific use.

Integrative medicine is different from *alternative medicine*, which means using an unproven practice instead of standard care. Using an alternative remedy in place of proven cancer treatment can be dangerous. In the United States, a federal agency, the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, funds research on which practices help and which do not.

The simplest safety step is also the most important. Tell your doctor, nurse or pharmacist about every herb, tea, powder and supplement you use, including ones from family or from other countries. Bring the labels. A good clinician will listen with respect, check for interactions and help you keep what is safe.

words.d: care that combines standard medicine with complementary practices that have evidence for a use
using an unproven practice instead of standard medical care
used together with standard medical care, not in place of it

look.title: Advice from a U.S. Health Agency
look.text: Tell all your health care providers about any complementary health approaches you use. Give them a full picture of what you do to manage your health. This will help ensure coordinated and safe care.
look.cite: National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH), "Tell Your Health Care Providers" guidance, about 2020
look.prompt: Why does the agency say to tell all your providers, not just one?

check.q: How is integrative medicine different from alternative medicine?
choices: Integrative adds proven practices to standard care; alternative replaces standard care
check.why: Integrative medicine combines evidence-based practices with standard care; alternative medicine uses them instead of it.

check.q: What does the word complementary mean in medicine?
choices: Used in place of standard care
check.why: Complementary means used together with standard care, not in place of it.

check.q: What is the most important safety step the reading names?
choices: Telling your doctor, nurse or pharmacist about every herb and supplement

check.why: The reading says the simplest and most important step is telling your clinicians everything you take.
